claims.text: The proposed multiscale approach explicitly decomposes lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr.
The approach will reduce total thermal-conductivity prediction error by at least 20% relative to Debye-temperature or DFT-elasticity-based models.
Separately accounting for temperature-dependent phonon scattering and electron transport will produce the claimed accuracy improvement.
The relevant HfNbTaTiZr specimens are single-phase and nearly defect-free bulk material.
Experimental variants of HfNbTaTiZr include material containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The proposed protocol couples advanced DFT, phonon Boltzmann transport, and first-principles electron-scattering calculations.
The model is intended to apply to pristine single-phase samples from 200 K to 1200 K.
Below 200 K, the lattice and electronic contributions are comparable.
DFT and explicit phonon-mode scattering calculations capture atomic-scale force-constant variations and local disorder.
Electronic band structure and scattering rates can be used to calculate the electronic thermal conductivity separately.

Direct simulation of temperature-dependent scattering distinguishes phonon-mediated from electron-mediated energy transport more effectively than Debye-temperature or bulk-elastic-property approximations.
Below 200 K, electronic thermal conductivity dominates lattice thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr.
Between 300 K and 1200 K, total thermal conductivity will be 10–17 W/(K·m).
Existing Debye- and DFT-elasticity-based analytical approaches do not separate lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions.
Existing analytical approaches typically have thermal-conductivity prediction errors of 30–50%.
The approach should generalize to concentrated alloys near the HfNbTaTiZr composition when they are nearly defect-free bulk materials.
Its applicability to samples with substantial microstructural defects or grain-boundary effects is undetermined.
Electrical-resistivity and isotopic-substitution measurements, combined with TDTR, can independently constrain lattice and electronic thermal transport.
Isotopic substitution preferentially changes phonon transport.
The hypothesis is falsified if component predictions differ from measurements by more than 20% or if the error reduction relative to baseline models is less than 20%.

contradictions.description: The conditions field describes the lattice and electronic contributions below 200 K as comparable, whereas the predicted outcome says the electronic contribution dominates in that regime.

A decisive prediction is made for temperatures below 200 K, but the proposed validation experiment only specifies measurements from 200 K to 1200 K, so it cannot directly test that low-temperature prediction.
